name: Vendor Lock-In
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: The Trap in the Convenience: Vendor Lock-In
lesson.summary: Vendor lock-in is what happens when a business's node infrastructure, tooling, and staff expertise become so tailored to one cloud provider that switching away is more disruptive and costly than tolerating that provider's terms, quietly reintroducing the single point of dependency blockchain was meant to avoid.
lesson.body:
Vendor lock-in is what happens after a business has already made the cloud choice described in the previous section and discovers, sometimes years later, that switching away from its chosen provider would be far more expensive and disruptive than it expected when it signed up. The convenience that made cloud infrastructure attractive in the first place, managed services, provider-specific tools, integrated monitoring and deployment pipelines, tends to be built around that specific provider's proprietary systems, not around open standards that would work identically somewhere else. Over time, a company's node infrastructure, deployment scripts, monitoring dashboards, and staff expertise all become tailored to one provider's particular way of doing things, and untangling that accumulated dependence turns out to be its own significant project.

The mechanism is worth being concrete about, because it rarely announces itself as a single dramatic moment. A team adopts a cloud provider's proprietary managed blockchain node service because it is genuinely easier to set up than running the software manually. Engineers build automation around that provider's specific interfaces. Data gets stored in that provider's storage format, accessed through that provider's specific tools. None of these individual decisions looks risky in isolation, each one is simply the path of least resistance at the time. But collectively they raise the cost of ever leaving, sometimes called switching cost, to the point where migrating to a different provider means rewriting automation, retraining staff, and risking downtime during the transition, a cost large enough that a company facing a price increase, a service degradation, or a policy change it dislikes may find it cheaper to simply tolerate the problem than to leave.

This matters more for blockchain infrastructure specifically than it might for an ordinary web application, because the underlying premise of blockchain technology, at least in its public form, is reducing reliance on any single trusted party. A business that decentralizes its application logic across a public blockchain but then concentrates all of its own node infrastructure, monitoring, and operational expertise inside one proprietary cloud provider has reintroduced a single point of dependency at the infrastructure layer, even though the ledger itself remains distributed among many independent participants. If that provider raises prices, changes its terms, experiences a prolonged outage, or discontinues the specific managed service the company depends on, the business faces real disruption despite the blockchain underneath being, in principle, resilient to exactly that kind of single-provider failure.

The practical defense against vendor lock-in is deliberate portability: favoring open standards and widely supported node software over a single provider's proprietary tooling, documenting infrastructure in a way that could be reproduced elsewhere, and periodically testing that a migration is actually possible rather than assuming it is. None of this eliminates the convenience tradeoff described under cloud versus on-premise, a business still generally benefits from cloud infrastructure's flexibility, but it keeps that convenience from quietly turning into permanent dependence on terms the business no longer controls.
